items.title: Reciprocity Service Return Card
items.description:
The last workshop exercise at the Futures 2.0 seminar last weekend (was it last weekend?) rested on the question that percolates around in my head: seriously..if there was universal basic income — pray tell — would you do? (Which begs the question as to why you aren't doing it now, but I don't want to get you all worked up.)

So — the exercise started with this form I sketched and then Rick made into somethign that actually looked like a form rather than a sketch.

The form looks like this so that one “falls into” the sense that this is a real artifact, the conceit being this:

In the UBI world, every year, or maybe twice a year, one has to do some kind of reciprocity service — contributing to the larger social organization (perhaps your Farm Operating Base pop. 2,604) in a meaningful way. So, you fill out this form with your proposed “service”. That is to say, you make a proposal as to what to do.

Of course, that doesn't mean proposing “sitting on my sofa playing Fortnite” is what you will do because presumably that is how you spend your time otherwise, if you're that kind of person. You might propose to teach a class on soil cultivation, or host a reading group on phenomenology, or a teach a class on Manga illustration. Something that reciprocates the value that you draw-down upon by otherwise and generally being self-indulgent for 2/3rds of the year.

The provocation was accepted by the seminar group and we ran the exercise with enthusiasm. I would say that it was a group of ringers — everyone there has the “giver” gene so they were excited to propose what they would do (or rather be doing in this world, I would guess.)

sections.title: Food For Thought

items.title: The Poetics of Design Fiction
items.description: I’ve been thinking about design fiction as more than “making up the future.” The authors of this academic-y paper — Markussen and Knutz — lay out a practical way to do design fiction by blending literary practice with design practice — so the story isn’t an accessory, it’s fully enmeshed in the method. They start with a sharper definition rooted in poetics and possible worlds, then back it up with four workshop projects co-developed with a Danish author. Their takeaway is this: good design fiction has craft in both directions, on the page and in the interface.

items.title: The Real Housing Crisis - Future Observatory Journal
items.description:
This piece from friend-of-the-blog Dan Hill resonated because when I was in Denver last weekend, Rafael pointed out how there was an area of downtown Denver that had “over built” and was somewhat latently occupied or something. That inspired a forward-facing wonderment: suppose there was a world where that space was used for indoor farming?

I know..I know..crazy, right?

Or maybe just weird enough such that sticking with that thought before dismissing is out of hand would be somehow...generative?

So..we sat with it and then the whole idea of a soil cultivation depository/repository led to the further design fiction of the Denver Public Biometic Hybridatarium so..I'm good with sufficiently weird to widen the conversation kind of things.

But, anyway — Dan's saying that he keeps hearing that the housing crisis is solved by “abundance” politics: loosen regulations, flood the market with more homes, and affordability will follow. But the piece makes a sharper point: there may not be a true housing shortage, and building more the same way won’t automatically fix affordability. Worse, the built environment’s extractive footprint means careless “build baby build” could wreck carbon budgets without delivering the housing outcomes we actually want. The real work, it argues, is changing the system settings and focusing emissions-aware, not-for-profit housing strategies.

The Near Future Laboratory is supported by its community and members. Join us on Patreon to support the newsletter, Office Hours, podcasts, Design Fiction experiments, and the ongoing Discord conversation around design, technology, creativity, and possible futures.

Patrons get an invitation to the Near Future Laboratory Discord and weekly Office Hours, where people bring projects, questions, half-formed ideas, and useful references into a generous working conversation.
